evidence.label: Nearly minimal maxima and positive minima of Littlewood polynomials
Asymptotically minimal maxima of real Littlewood polynomials

headline: Polynomials with only +1 and −1 coefficients can be almost perfectly flat on the unit circle.
scope: The results hold at every large enough length, with fresh signs at each length. They show existence only.
plain: A Littlewood polynomial has coefficients that are all +1 or −1. Its typical size on the unit circle is the square root of its length. One paper proves that its largest size can get as close to that as you like. Another paper claims the smallest size can get close too, for the same polynomial. The first paper also claims that merit factors of sign patterns grow without limit, disproving Turyn's conjecture.
doesNot: This does not give a way to find the signs, or say when the bounds start to hold.
origin: This result comes from an unreleased OpenAI model, published in the openai/math release on 6 October 2026.

scorecard.significanceWhy: It answers a real-sign flatness question from Erdős's problem lists and disproves Turyn's bounded-merit-factor conjecture.

explanation:
Take four signs: +1, +1, +1, −1. Use them as the coefficients of a polynomial, P(z) = 1 + z + z² − z³. Now let z travel once around the unit circle. That is the circle of complex numbers whose size is exactly 1. At each point, measure the size of P(z). At z = 1 the size is 2. The average of the squared size is exactly 4, the sum of the squared signs. So the natural typical size is √4 = 2.

The size does not stay at 2. It climbs to about 2.66 and drops to about 0.96. That is about 1.33 times the typical size at the top, and 0.48 times at the bottom. A search of all 16 sign patterns of length 4 finds none with a lower top.

A polynomial whose coefficients are all +1 or −1 is called a real Littlewood polynomial. Its length N is the number of coefficients. Its typical size on the circle is always √N, for the reason above. The top can never sit below √N. Call a family of such polynomials ultraflat if size divided by √N gets uniformly close to 1 as N grows. Uniformly means at every point of the circle at once, top and bottom together.

Paul Erdős asked in 1957 whether such polynomials can stay between two fixed multiples of √N. A construction of Shapiro and Rudin gives a top of at most √(2N) when N is a power of two. In 2020, Balister, Bollobás, Morris, Sahasrabudhe and Tiba built flat ones of every degree from two up. Their sizes stay between two fixed positive multiples of √N. But the multiples do not approach 1. A real-sign version of an Erdős question asked whether the top always stays at least a fixed fraction above √N.

The one obstacle is that the coefficients must be plain signs. With complex coefficients of size 1, each coefficient can point in any direction. Jean-Pierre Kahane used that freedom to build ultraflat polynomials in 1980. Real signs leave no such room. The papers first build coefficients anywhere between −1 and 1 that give a nearly flat curve. They then round each coefficient to +1 or −1 while keeping the error small.

Three papers make the claims. The September paper proves that the top can be pushed to within any small margin of √N. This holds for every large enough length, not just special ones. A second paper claims to add a floor of √N/16 for the same polynomial. The third paper claims the full ultraflat result. For any small ε, it claims signs whose size stays between (1 − ε)√N and (1 + ε)√N everywhere. That includes the real points z = 1 and z = −1. The signs may be chosen afresh at each length.

A consequence concerns the merit factor of a sign pattern. Slide the pattern against itself and record each overlap total. For +1, +1, +1, −1 the totals are 1, 0 and −1. The merit factor is N² divided by twice the sum of their squares. Here that is 16 divided by 4, giving 4. At length 13, the best of all 8,192 patterns scores 169/12, about 14.08. Turyn's conjecture said merit factors stay bounded over all patterns. In 2013, Jedwab, Katz and Schmidt reached families with limiting merit factor 6.342061…. The September paper claims the largest merit factor at length N tends to infinity. That would disprove Turyn's conjecture. It gives no rate of growth.

The results say such signs exist. They give no useful rate and no efficient way to find the signs. They also do not say how large N must be before each bound holds.

How sure is this? A computer proof checker called Lean has checked the September main theorem. That is the top bound of (1 + η)√N at every large length. Lean also covers a related average form of flatness for one family. The Lean scope note does not list the merit-factor consequence. The √N/16 floor and the two-sided ultraflat theorem are outside the Lean check. No specialist review has been published.
hypeCheck: Major if the papers hold. Lean covers only the upper bound on the maximum and a related average flatness statement. The two-sided ultraflat theorem and the merit-factor consequence are not in the Lean scope note. No specialist review is published.

glossary.meaning: A polynomial whose coefficients are all +1 or −1 (real signs, in this entry).
The complex numbers whose size is exactly 1.
A family whose size divided by √N gets uniformly close to 1 on the whole unit circle as the length N grows.
Staying between two fixed positive multiples of √N everywhere on the unit circle.
N² divided by twice the sum of squared overlap totals of a sign pattern with its shifted copies.
The conjecture that merit factors of sign patterns stay bounded over all lengths.
